title: The correspondent cut the limit without warning
explain:
A correspondent cuts an intraday credit limit without warning.
The routing engine keeps feeding the same corridor, EUR 300,000 of payments queue up, and rejects arrive that nobody can explain.
The corridor was fine yesterday. The limit changed, and the engine never noticed.

Here's how that happens:

→ Correspondent cuts the intraday limit
→ Engine keeps feeding the same corridor
→ Payments queue and rejects arrive unexplained

The assumption was:
"Routing rules are written for the quiet day."

Good routing rules are written for the bad day, not the quiet one: a correspondent can cut an intraday credit limit without warning, and an engine that keeps feeding the same corridor will queue payments and generate rejects it cannot explain. Build the rules with eligibility checks, fallback routes, a defined decision order, and an audit trail naming the affected payments and the reason.

A routing decision nobody can reconstruct is a control failure, not a routing outcome.

BA Takeaway

Build eligibility checks, fallback routes, a defined decision order and an audit trail into the routing rules. When a limit changes, the engine re-routes and records which payments were affected and why.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Corridor eligibility check
→ Fallback route
→ Defined decision order
→ Audit trail naming payments and reason

The real requirement isn't "Did the payment route?"

It's "What evidence proves why it routed that way, and what happens when the limit changes?"

Have you ever watched an engine keep feeding a corridor whose limit had just been cut?
takeaway: A routing decision nobody can reconstruct is a control failure, not a routing outcome.

title: The customer cut-off is 3:25 PM. The deadline is 4:00 PM.
explain:
A customer submits a EUR 70,000 payment at 3:30 PM and expects it out today.
The downstream deadline is 4:00 PM.
The payment misses the day, and the customer is told the cut-off was 3:25 PM, a time that appears nowhere in the product.

Here's how that happens:

→ Downstream deadline 4:00 PM
→ Screening takes 20 minutes
→ Buffer takes 15 minutes
→ Customer cut-off lands at 3:25 PM

The assumption was:
"A cut-off is a time on the clock."

A cut-off time is a calculated risk decision, not a time on the clock, and it starts from the downstream deadline, subtracting screening time, buffer, processing capacity, file size, treasury funding and expected rejections. In the worked example a 4:00 PM downstream deadline minus a 15-minute buffer minus 20 minutes of screening gives a 3:25 PM customer cut-off, with guaranteed service until 3:00 PM, best effort until 3:25 PM and next-day service after that.

A cut-off is a calculated risk decision, not a time on the clock.

BA Takeaway

Calculate the cut-off backwards from the downstream deadline, subtracting screening, buffer, processing capacity, file size, funding and expected rejections. Then publish the tiers: guaranteed until 3:00 PM, best effort until 3:25 PM, next-day service after that.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Downstream deadline
→ Screening time
→ Buffer
→ Processing capacity and file size
→ Treasury funding
→ Expected rejections

The real requirement isn't "What time is the cut-off?"

It's "What evidence proves the cut-off leaves enough time for screening, buffer and funding?"

Have you ever missed a cut-off that was calculated, not published?
takeaway: A payment BA should ask what time the payment must be out of the file, whether the deadline is hard, and whether tiers are needed in the requirements.

title: The cheapest rail that still arrives on time
explain:
A debtor bank must send a EUR 75,000 payment, and the treasurer wants the cheapest route.
The cheapest route takes three days.
The beneficiary needs the money tomorrow, and the cheapest rail that arrives on time is not the cheapest rail.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment to send, EUR 75,000
→ Cheapest route takes three days
→ Beneficiary needs it tomorrow
→ Routing rules pick the cheapest rail that arrives on time

The assumption was:
"Cheapest is always best."

A debtor bank looks for the cheapest way to reach the beneficiary on time. When the receiver sits in the same country the payment goes through the local clearing and settlement mechanism or the local real time gross settlement system, and when the receiver sits abroad it goes through SWIFT. Routing rules set up in the payment engine apply that choice automatically, including for bulk MT101 and pain.001 files.

Cheapest on time, not cheapest at any cost.

BA Takeaway

Write the routing rules as cheapest on time. Same country goes through the local clearing mechanism or the local RTGS, abroad goes through SWIFT, and the payment engine applies the choice automatically, including for bulk MT101 and pain.001 files.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Same country, local rail
→ Another country, SWIFT
→ Value date required
→ Routing rules in the engine

The real requirement isn't "What is the cheapest rail?"

It's "What evidence proves the chosen rail is the cheapest one that still arrives on time?"

Have you ever picked the cheapest rail and missed the value date?
takeaway: Routing rules set up in the payment engine apply that choice automatically, including for bulk MT101 and pain.001 files.

explain:
A SEPA payment of EUR 20,000 failed.
The team raised it as a reject and asked the customer to resend it.
The customer had already been debited, and the money came back twice.

Here is what happened:

→ pain.001 instruction raised
→ pacs.008 sent for EUR 20,000
→ Payment settles
→ pacs.004 return arrives after settlement

The requirement said:
"Treat every failed SEPA payment the same way."

So the team followed the reject path for a payment that had already settled.

Why?

In SEPA, timing is the whole distinction. A reject happens before settlement and is reported with pacs.002. A return happens after settlement and uses pacs.004. A reject means the money never moved, so resend is safe. A return means the money moved and came back, so resending without checking credits the customer twice.

The stage decides the path.

BA Takeaway

Before and after settlement are different worlds, so keep them separate:

→ Reject before settlement, pacs.002
→ Return after settlement, pacs.004
→ Funds position confirmed before any resend

The real requirement is not "When did it fail?"

It is "What evidence proves whether the funds moved, before we tell the customer to resend?"

Have you ever seen a return handled as a reject and the customer paid twice?
takeaway: The stage decides the path.

explain:
A customer tried to pay GBP 4,500.
It failed three times.
Each time the screen said the same thing: declined.

Here is what happened:

→ First attempt fails on a timeout, no response arrives in time
→ Second attempt fails on a limit, the amount exceeds the daily limit
→ Third attempt fails on a downstream error after acceptance
→ Customer is told declined on all three attempts

The requirement said:
"Show one generic failure message for every failed payment."

So the customer kept retrying the same payment, and support kept blaming the issuer.

Why?

A timeout, a limit failure and a downstream failure need completely different actions. A timeout may succeed on retry, a limit needs a higher limit or a split payment, and a downstream failure needs operations to trace the payment after acceptance. One label hides the cause and sends everyone down the wrong path.

A failure label is not a diagnosis.

BA Takeaway

The cause decides who acts and what the customer is told, so keep the causes separate:

→ Issuer decline and validation failure
→ Limit failure and timeout failure
→ Connectivity, risk and downstream failure

The real requirement is not "When do we show declined?"

It is "What evidence proves which cause failed, and who must act on it?"

Have you ever chased a declined payment that turned out to be a timeout?
takeaway: A failure label is not a diagnosis.

title: EUR 18,000 recalled by camt.056, and the bank waited for a pacs.004
explain:
A customer asks for EUR 18,000 back after a payment was credited in error.
The bank sends a camt.056 recall request.
Then it waits for a pacs.004, and nothing arrives for a week.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment already settled and credited to the beneficiary
→ camt.056 sent, asking the beneficiary bank to return it
→ The team treats the camt.056 as if it moves the money
→ No pacs.004 ever comes, because the beneficiary bank has not agreed

The assumption was:
"A recall request is a return."

Why?

A pacs.004 returns a payment that has already settled, sending the funds back along the chain to the originator. A camt.056 requests a recall, asking the beneficiary bank to return a payment already credited. The two are often confused, yet they do opposite jobs: the pacs.004 moves the money back, while the camt.056 asks for the money back.

Asking ≠ Returning.

BA Takeaway

Track the recall and the return as two separate things, and never promise the customer on the request alone.

Keep these controls separate:

→ camt.056 recall requested
→ Beneficiary bank decision on the recall
→ pacs.004 return actually received
→ Funds credited back to the customer

The real requirement isn't "Did we send the recall?"

It's "What evidence proves the funds actually came back, not just that we asked for them?"

Have you seen a customer promised a refund on a recall request that was never agreed?
takeaway: The two are often confused, yet they do opposite jobs: the pacs.004 moves the money back, while the camt.056 asks for the money back.

title: EUR 12,000 paid twice from one pacs.008 file
explain:
A bulk pacs.008 file pays a supplier EUR 12,000.
The same supplier is paid EUR 12,000 again the next day.
The file contained the same transaction twice.

Here's how that happens:

→ pain.001 carries one instruction more than once
→ pacs.008 file built with the same payment inside it twice
→ No duplicate check runs before processing
→ Both payments settle, and the supplier is paid double

The assumption was:
"The file is clean because the customer sent it."

Why?

Every payment inside a pacs.008 file carries its own unique identification, and that identifier is the control that catches a file containing the same transaction twice before it is processed. The check matters because a bulk file such as a pain.001 can carry one instruction more than once, and paying it twice is a real loss.

Duplicate detection is a pre-processing discipline, not a post-payment investigation.

A file received ≠ A file checked.

BA Takeaway

Run the duplicate check on unique identification before any payment in the file is processed.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Unique identification on every payment
→ Duplicate check before processing
→ Payments released for settlement
→ Recovery if a duplicate slips through

The real requirement isn't "Did we process the file?"

It's "What evidence proves the duplicate check ran on every payment before settlement?"

Have you seen a supplier paid twice because a file was trusted without a check?
takeaway: Duplicate detection is therefore a pre-processing discipline, not a post-payment investigation.

title: EUR 22,000 SEPA payment rejected, and the beneficiary bank never knew it existed
explain:
A customer sends EUR 22,000 by SEPA credit transfer.
The beneficiary calls to say nothing arrived.
The beneficiary bank says it never saw the payment at all.

Here's how that happens:

→ Originator bank sends pacs.008 into the clearing and settlement mechanism
→ The mechanism validates it against its own rules and it fails
→ A pacs.002 rejection goes back to the originator bank
→ The beneficiary bank is never told the payment existed

The assumption was:
"A rejection means the beneficiary bank turned it down."

Why?

In a SEPA credit transfer, the pacs.008 passes through the clearing and settlement mechanism on its way to the beneficiary bank, and the mechanism validates it against its own rules. A failure at that stage comes back as a pacs.002, so the payment never reaches the beneficiary bank and that bank stays unaware of it. A fault spotted later, at the beneficiary bank itself, travels back as a pacs.004 return instead, because receipt has already happened by then.

A pacs.002 rejection ≠ A beneficiary bank decision.

BA Takeaway

Read the rejection to find where it failed: mechanism, or beneficiary bank.

Keep these controls separate:

→ pacs.002 rejection at the mechanism, beneficiary bank unaware
→ pacs.004 return at the beneficiary bank, receipt already happened
→ Reason for the failure at the right stage
→ Customer told which stage stopped it

The real requirement isn't "Was the payment rejected?"

It's "What evidence proves we know which stage rejected it, and told the customer the truth about it?"

Have you seen a customer chase a beneficiary bank that never saw their payment?
takeaway: A fault spotted later, at the beneficiary bank itself, travels back as a pacs.004 return instead, because receipt has already happened by then.

title: EUR 4,000 collection due Friday, creditor bank closed, collection never sent
explain:
A creditor plans a EUR 4,000 collection for Friday.
The debtor bank is open. The scheme is open.
The creditor bank is closed for a holiday.
The collection is never sent.

Here is how that happens:

→ Due date arrives, Friday
→ Debtor PSP open, ready to debit
→ Creditor PSP closed on the due date
→ Collection cannot be submitted into the scheme that day

The assumption was:
"If the debtor bank is open, the collection can run."

If the creditor PSP is closed on the due date, the collection cannot be submitted into the scheme on that date, even if the debtor PSP is open.

Why?

The creditor-side processing constraint moves the collection to the next business day. The creditor must plan for its own closure days, not just the debtor's, because its own calendar is a hard gate on submission.

Your own holiday stops your own collection.

Why does a collection fail when the debtor bank is open and ready?

BA Takeaway

Plan collections against your own calendar first, and move the due date before the holiday, not after the failure.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Creditor PSP calendar, the hard gate on submission
→ Debtor PSP calendar, the gate on the debit
→ Scheme calendar, the gate on clearing and settlement
→ Next business day, where the collection lands

Check all three calendars before setting a due date, and show the creditor closure on the collection plan.

The real requirement is not "Is the debtor bank open?"

It is "What evidence proves every calendar in the chain is open on the due date?"

Have you missed a collection because your own bank was closed?
takeaway: The creditor must plan for its own closure days, not just the debtor's, because its own calendar is a hard gate on submission.

title: EUR 4,000 collection due Friday, debtor bank closed, debit lands Monday
explain:
A creditor sends a EUR 4,000 collection for Friday.
The creditor bank is open. The scheme is open.
The debtor bank is closed for a holiday.
The debit lands on Monday, and the creditor had promised the money for Friday.

Here is how that happens:

→ Due date arrives, Friday
→ Creditor PSP open, collection submitted
→ Debtor PSP closed on the due date
→ Debtor account cannot be debited that day, debit moves to Monday

The assumption was:
"Submitted on Friday means debited on Friday."

If the debtor PSP is closed on the due date, the debtor account cannot be debited on that date, so the debit moves to the next business day the debtor PSP is open.

Why?

The collection is not lost, but the timing shifts, and the creditor must know which date the debit will actually happen. This is why the debtor PSP calendar matters as much as the creditor's: it fixes the real debit date.

Submitted is not debited.

Why does a Friday collection debit on Monday?

BA Takeaway

Promise the real debit date, taken from the debtor PSP calendar, not the due date.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Submission date, when the collection enters the scheme
→ Debtor PSP calendar, what fixes the real debit date
→ Actual debit date, the next business day the debtor PSP is open
→ Customer promise, dated from the actual debit date

Show the actual debit date beside the due date on every collection.

The real requirement is not "Was the collection submitted on time?"

It is "What evidence proves the debit date the creditor promised?"

Have you promised Friday money that debited on Monday?
takeaway: The debtor PSP calendar matters as much as the creditor's: it fixes the real debit date.

title: EUR 12,000 in collections due, both banks open, clearing closed
explain:
EUR 12,000 in collections is due today.
Both banks are open and working.
Nothing settles.
The clearing mechanism between them is closed.

Here is how that happens:

→ Due date arrives, collections ready
→ Creditor PSP open, debtor PSP open
→ Clearing and settlement mechanism closed on the due date
→ Collections cannot be submitted and settled that day

The assumption was:
"If both banks are open, the payment can settle."

The clearing and settlement mechanism is the infrastructure that moves collections between the creditor PSP and the debtor PSP.

Why?

If it is closed on the due date, the collections cannot be submitted and settled that day, even when both banks are open and working. Both banks being open is not enough: the infrastructure between them must also be open, so the mechanism's calendar belongs in every collection plan.

Two open banks, one closed road between them.

Why does nothing settle when both banks are open?

BA Takeaway

Check the infrastructure calendar as well as the bank calendars, and plan the due date around all three.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Creditor PSP calendar, open or closed
→ Debtor PSP calendar, open or closed
→ Clearing mechanism calendar, the infrastructure between them
→ Settlement date, only when all three are open

Show all three calendars on the collection plan, with the mechanism calendar beside the bank calendars.

The real requirement is not "Are the banks open?"

It is "What evidence proves the infrastructure between them is open too?"

Have you watched two open banks fail to settle?
takeaway: Both banks being open is not enough: the infrastructure between them must also be open.

title: EUR 950 debited with permission, customer wants it back in week seven
explain:
A debtor authorised a direct debit of EUR 950.
Seven weeks after the debit, the debtor asks for the money back.
The creditor calls it an exception.
It is not an exception. It is a scheme right.

Here is how that happens:

→ Debtor authorises the collection of EUR 950
→ Debit happens, collection completes
→ Week seven, debtor asks for a refund
→ Creditor treats the request as a dispute

The assumption was:
"An authorised debit cannot be refunded."

When a debtor authorised a SEPA Direct Debit collection, they can ask for a refund within eight weeks of the debit date.

Why?

The eight-week rule is the stated scheme position, but the exact application can vary by jurisdiction, so it must be checked against the current rulebook. A refund inside this window is a normal scheme right, not an exception, and treating it as a dispute delays a right the debtor already holds.

Authorised does not mean unrefundable.

Why does a lawful refund request get treated as a dispute?

BA Takeaway

Handle an authorised refund as a normal scheme right, inside its eight-week window.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Authorised collection, the debit the debtor agreed to
→ Eight-week window, the refund right from the debit date
→ Rulebook check, exact application per jurisdiction
→ Refund, a normal scheme right, not an exception

Show the eight-week deadline on every authorised debit, and route refund requests to the refund process, not the dispute process.

The real requirement is not "Was the debit authorised?"

It is "What evidence proves the refund was handled inside the scheme window?"

Have you seen a scheme right treated as a dispute?
takeaway: A refund inside this window is a normal scheme right, not an exception.

title: EUR 1,100 taken without authorisation, claim arrives in month twelve
explain:
A debtor finds a direct debit of EUR 1,100 on the statement.
The debtor never authorised it.
Twelve months have passed.
The creditor says it is too late. It is not.

Here is how that happens:

→ Direct debit of EUR 1,100 taken, no authorisation behind it
→ Debtor discovers it months later
→ Claim filed in month twelve
→ Creditor handles it as an authorised refund, and refuses it

The assumption was:
"All refunds work the same way, with the same window."

When a debtor says a direct debit was never authorised, they can claim a refund for up to 13 months after the debit.

Why?

The 13-month period is the stated scheme position, and the precise legal and scheme conditions must be checked against the current rulebook. An unauthorised claim is a different process from an authorised refund, with a longer window and different evidence, so the two must never be handled as one case type.

Unauthorised is a different case, not a late authorised one.

Why does a twelve-month claim get refused as too late?

BA Takeaway

Route unauthorised claims to the unauthorised process, with its 13-month window and its own evidence.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Authorised refund, eight weeks, debtor agreed
→ Unauthorised claim, up to 13 months, debtor never agreed
→ Evidence, different for each case type
→ Rulebook check, precise conditions per case

Show the case type on every refund request, and never judge an unauthorised claim by the authorised window.

The real requirement is not "How long ago was the debit?"

It is "What evidence proves this claim was handled under the right case type?"

title: EUR 2,000 comes back, the ledger books it as the wrong event
explain:
EUR 2,000 comes back after a direct debit.
The ledger books it as a refund.
It was a return, started by the debtor bank because the account could not be debited.
The timeline, the message and the accounting are all wrong now.

Here is how that happens:

→ Collection of EUR 2,000 presented
→ Debtor PSP cannot debit the account, sends it back
→ Team books it as a refund, debtor asked for money back
→ Real event was a return, different initiator, different rules

The assumption was:
"Money back is money back. One event covers them all."

A return, a refund and a reversal are three different money-back events with different initiators, reasons, messages and accounting treatment.

Why?

A return is started by the debtor PSP, usually because the account cannot be debited. A refund is started by the debtor asking for money back. A reversal is started by the creditor PSP to undo a collection. Treating them as the same thing causes wrong messages, wrong timelines and wrong ledger entries, so the three must be modelled as separate events.

Three events, three initiators, three treatments.

Why does one money-back booking corrupt the message, the timeline and the ledger?

BA Takeaway

Model return, refund and reversal as separate events, and let the initiator decide which one it is.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Return, started by the debtor PSP, account cannot be debited
→ Refund, started by the debtor asking for money back
→ Reversal, started by the creditor PSP to undo a collection
→ Messages, timelines and ledger entries, different for each

Require the initiator on every money-back event before it is booked.

The real requirement is not "Did the money come back?"

It is "What evidence proves which of the three events brought it back?"

Have you booked a return as a refund?
takeaway: Treating them as the same thing causes wrong messages, wrong timelines and wrong ledger entries.

title: EUR 1,500 return and EUR 1,500 refund land the same day, team nets them
explain:
Two EUR 1,500 amounts land on the same day.
One is a return, one is a refund.
The team nets them and closes both cases.
Both cases are still open, and both are now wrong.

Here is how that happens:

→ Collection presented for EUR 1,500
→ Debtor bank sends it back, insufficient funds, pacs.004
→ Debtor asks for an authorised collection to be repaid, refund
→ Both arrive the same day and look similar

The assumption was:
"Same day, same amount, same event."

A SEPA Direct Debit return and a refund can arrive on the same day and look similar, but they are different business events.

Why?

A return happens when the debtor bank sends the collection back, for example because the account has insufficient funds, and it travels as a pacs.004, while a refund happens when the debtor asks for an authorised collection to be repaid. Each has its own trigger, timeline and accounting treatment, so the system must handle them as separate events even when they land together.

Same day is not the same event.

Why does netting two same-day amounts close two cases that are both still open?

BA Takeaway

Handle return and refund as separate events, even when they land together.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Return, debtor bank sends it back, pacs.004, insufficient funds
→ Refund, debtor asks for an authorised collection to be repaid
→ Trigger, timeline and accounting, different for each

Never net a return against a refund, and show each on its own case line.

The real requirement is not "Did the amounts match?"

It is "What evidence proves each event was handled on its own trigger and timeline?"

title: EUR 3,200 collection returned, reason code unread for four days
explain:
A collection of EUR 3,200 is returned.
The pacs.004 carries a reason code.
Nobody on the returns team can read it consistently.
The creditor finds out four days late, with no clear explanation.

Here is how that happens:

→ Collection returned, pacs.004 arrives
→ Reason code inside pacs.004 explains why
→ Returns team interprets the code differently each time
→ Creditor learns days late, with no clear explanation

The assumption was:
"The return message is enough. The code will explain itself."

When a direct debit collection is returned, the pacs.004 carries a reason code that explains why, and the scheme sets a timeline for when the return must happen.

Why?

The creditor needs to learn about the return quickly and understand whether the collection can be presented again. If the returns team cannot interpret the reason codes consistently, creditors find out days late with no clear explanation, so code interpretation is an operational capability, not a back-office nicety.

An unread code is an unexplained return.

Why does the creditor learn about a return four days late?

BA Takeaway

Make reason-code interpretation a trained, consistent capability, and tell the creditor fast.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Reason code, in pacs.004, explaining why
→ Scheme timeline, when the return must happen
→ Creditor notice, fast, with the explanation
→ Re-present decision, can the collection be presented again

Show the code, its plain-language meaning, and the re-present answer on every return the same day it arrives.

The real requirement is not "Did the pacs.004 arrive?"

It is "What evidence proves the creditor was told quickly, in words they can act on?"

Have you seen a return sit unread while the creditor waited?
takeaway: If the returns team cannot interpret the reason codes consistently, creditors find out days late with no clear explanation.

title: 90 percent of a remittance file lands in repair
explain:
A corporate customer sends a daily remittance file with thousands of supplier payments, worth EUR 2.4 million.

Around 90 percent of the payments land in the manual repair queue.

The file is on time. The money is not.

Here is how it happens:

→ File arrives with thousands of supplier payments
→ Account numbers fail the modulus check
→ Remittance information arrives incomplete or inconsistent
→ Payments drop into manual repair
→ The repair queue becomes the bottleneck

The requirement said:
"The repair team will handle the exceptions."

Why?

The data is bad at the source. The queue is a symptom of bad input, not of slow repair. Adding repair staff only feeds a bigger queue.

The queue is a symptom, not the problem.

BA Takeaway

Fix the data at the source. Repair capacity is the last control, not the first.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Source data quality
→ Validation at capture
→ Repair capacity

The real requirement is not "How fast can we repair?"

It is "What evidence proves the file is clean before it is accepted?"

Have you seen a repair queue grow because the source data was never fixed?
takeaway: The queue is a symptom, not the problem. Fix the data at the source.

title: camt.055 sent after settlement: EUR 75,000 already gone
explain:
A customer asks to cancel a EUR 75,000 payment.

The team sends camt.055 to stop it.

The payment already settled and the beneficiary is already credited.

Here is how it happens:

→ Payment settles and beneficiary is credited
→ camt.055 sent to stop the payment
→ camt.055 is rejected
→ camt.029 arrives carrying RJCR
→ Recovery switches to the return route

The assumption was:
"Send camt.055 to stop it."

Why?

Cancellation and return are governed by lifecycle position, not by urgency. camt.055 can stop a payment only while it remains before settlement. Once settlement and credit have completed, the only route back is a camt.056 requesting the funds, or a pacs.004 carrying them back.

camt.055 stops a payment. It cannot undo one.

BA Takeaway

Establish the lifecycle stage before choosing the message. The disciplined move is to locate the payment first, then pick cancellation or return.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Lifecycle stage of the payment
→ Cancellation message
→ Return route

The real requirement is not "How do we cancel it?"

It is "What evidence proves where the payment sits before we choose the message?"

Have you sent a cancellation for a payment that had already settled?
takeaway: camt.055 stops a payment. It cannot undo one. Check the lifecycle first.

title: pacs.009 cover rejected, but the EUR 40,000 payment had not failed
explain:
A pacs.009 cover is rejected with FF01, invalid account number.

The team assumes the payment failed and re-credits the customer EUR 40,000.

The funds were still held by the bank. The customer is now paid twice.

Here is how it happens:

→ pacs.009 COV rejected, FF01
→ Team reads the rejection as a failed payment
→ Customer is re-credited EUR 40,000
→ Funds are still held by the bank
→ Customer is paid twice, or funds go to the wrong account

The assumption was:
"A rejected cover means the payment failed."

Why?

A rejected cover does not by itself prove the underlying payment failed. The credit advice may simply carry a wrong account mapping while the funds remain held. The reason code governs the next move.

A rejection code is a clue, not a verdict.

BA Takeaway

Investigate the reason code before re-crediting. The rejection alone must never trigger the refund.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Reason code
→ Funds position
→ Re-credit decision

The real requirement is not "Was something rejected?"

It is "What evidence proves the payment failed before we re-credit?"

Have you seen a re-credit go out before anyone checked what the reason code actually meant?
takeaway: A rejection code is a clue, not a verdict. The rejection alone must never trigger the refund.

title: camt.056 sent, EUR 60,000 stuck in silence
explain:
A bank asks for EUR 60,000 back with a camt.056.

Nobody answers.

The payment sits in a waiting state, neither completed nor rejected, and the funds just hang.

Here is how it happens:

→ camt.056 sent to request the return
→ No answer arrives
→ Payment sits waiting, neither completed nor rejected
→ No status check is planned
→ No escalation route exists

The assumption was:
"The beneficiary will answer."

Why?

An unanswered camt.056 leaves the payment stuck while the return of funds hangs. The exit is a camt.029 status check, followed by waiting for a response or escalating when the beneficiary does not reply within the agreed time.

Every waiting state needs a way out.

BA Takeaway

Design every waiting state in advance with an entry, an exit, a time limit, a status check and an escalation route.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Waiting state and its time limit
→ Status check with camt.029
→ Escalation route

The real requirement is not "How long do we wait?"

It is "What evidence proves we know what happens if nobody ever replies?"

Have you seen a payment sit in a waiting state with no agreed way out?
takeaway: Every waiting state needs a way out. Design the exit before the wait begins.

title: The Rs. 12,000 chargeback that changed hands three times
explain:
A cardholder disputes a Rs. 12,000 transaction.

The issuer raises it. The merchant fights it with representment evidence.

The loss moves between issuer, acquirer and merchant, and the reason code decides who holds it at each stage.

Here is how it happens:

→ Cardholder disputes the transaction
→ Issuer raises the chargeback with the scheme
→ Acquirer and merchant respond with representment evidence
→ Scheme applies its timelines and reason codes
→ Financial impact moves between issuer, acquirer and merchant

The assumption was:
"The reason code is just a label."

Why?

The reason code decides what evidence is needed and who bears the loss at each stage. The wrong code means the wrong evidence, and the wrong party pays.

The reason code is the case, not a label on it.

BA Takeaway

Start every chargeback from the reason code, and build the evidence around what that code demands.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Reason code
→ Representment evidence
→ Scheme timelines

The real requirement is not "Was the transaction disputed?"

It is "What evidence proves we hold the evidence the reason code demands?"

Have you seen a chargeback lost because the team argued the facts and ignored the reason code?
takeaway: The reason code is the case, not a label on it. It decides the evidence and who bears the loss.

title: EUR 80,000 came back, but the return was sent to the wrong bank
explain:
A beneficiary bank returned EUR 80,000.
The originator bank waited for it.
The return never arrived, because it was sent straight to the originator instead of back through the chain.

Here's how that happens:

→ pacs.008 sent EUR 80,000 to the beneficiary
→ Beneficiary bank returns it with pacs.004
→ Return sent directly to the originator, skipping the intermediary
→ Originator cannot match it, and the funds sit unreconciled

The assumption was:
"A return goes straight back to where the payment came from."
In a three-bank chain, the return must travel the chain in reverse.

Why?

The intermediary that received the pacs.004 must send a new pacs.004 back to the originator bank, carrying the reference to the original payment. Skip the intermediary and the link between the return and the original payment breaks.

A return travels the chain in reverse, or it travels nowhere.

What proves the return reached the bank that sent the payment?

BA Takeaway

Treat every return as a chain, not a single hop. Each bank forwards the pacs.004 to the bank that sent it the payment, with the original reference intact, so the originator can match it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Return status
→ Original references
→ Funds received and reconciled

The real requirement isn't "Has the money come back?"

It's "What evidence proves the return reached the bank that sent the payment?"

Have you ever chased a return that was sent to the wrong bank in the chain?
takeaway: A return travels the chain in reverse, or it travels nowhere.

title: EUR 80,000 arrived back, but no one could say which payment it was
explain:
EUR 80,000 arrived back at the originator bank.
The credit sat in the account for two days.
No one could say which payment it belonged to.

Here's how that happens:

→ → pacs.004 arrives as a credit
→ → Original instruction identification missing from the trail
→ → Original end-to-end identification missing too
→ → Reconciliation cannot place the credit

The assumption was:
"A credit is a credit. Book it and move on."
A credit with no story cannot be booked against any payment.

Why?

A pacs.004 carries the original instruction identification and the original end-to-end identification, and those two references tie it to the payment it returns. Without them the return is only a credit, and reconciliation cannot prove which payment it belongs to.

Without those references a return is only a credit with no story.

What proves this credit belongs to that payment?

BA Takeaway

Never book a return on amount alone. Match the original instruction identification and the original end-to-end identification first, and hold the credit unreconciled until both references check out.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Original instruction identification
→ Original end-to-end identification
→ Reconciliation match

The real requirement isn't "Has the money come back?"

It's "What evidence proves this credit belongs to that payment?"

takeaway: Without those references a return is only a credit with no story.

title: EUR 120,000 recalled, and the recall had to cross three banks
explain:
A customer asked for EUR 120,000 back.
The payment had already crossed an intermediary bank.
One message could not bring it back, because the money sat at the end of a chain.

Here's how that happens:

→ → Originator bank sends camt.056 to the intermediary
→ → Intermediary forwards camt.056 to the beneficiary bank
→ → Beneficiary bank checks whether the recall is feasible
→ → Beneficiary bank returns funds with pacs.004
→ → Intermediary sends pacs.004 back to the originator

The assumption was:
"Send one recall and the money comes back."
A recall is a chain of messages, not a single message.

Why?

Each bank in the chain must act in turn. The funds come back only when every bank in the chain acts, so a recall that stops at any link leaves the money where it is.

A recall is a chain of messages, not a single message.

What proves every bank in the chain acted on the recall?

BA Takeaway

Send the camt.056 through the same chain the payment took. Track the recall at each bank, wait for the camt.029 answer, and only then expect the pacs.004.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Recall request sent
→ Response received
→ Funds returned
→ Books reconciled

The real requirement isn't "Has the recall been sent?"

It's "What evidence proves every bank in the chain acted on the recall?"

Have you ever waited on a recall that stopped at one bank in the chain?
takeaway: A recall is a chain of messages, not a single message.

title: EUR 60,000 returned, and both ends claimed the return was theirs to start
explain:
EUR 60,000 had to come back.
The originator bank said it would start the return.
The beneficiary bank said it would start the return.
Both were right, and the team argued about it for a day.

Here's how that happens:

→ → Originator side recalls the payment
→ → Beneficiary side rejects a payment it cannot apply
→ → Both use the same message, pacs.004
→ → Only the initiating bank and the reason differ

The assumption was:
"A return can only start at one end."
A return can be started from either end of the payment.

Why?

The originator side starts a pacs.004 when it recalls or reverses a payment, and the beneficiary side starts one when it rejects or returns a payment it cannot apply. The message is identical in both cases.

The message is identical in both cases. Only the initiating bank and the reason differ.

What proves who started this return, and why?

BA Takeaway

Read the initiating bank and the reason code on the pacs.004, not the message name. The name tells you it is a return. The starter and the reason tell you what happened.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Initiating bank
→ Reason code
→ Original payment reference

The real requirement isn't "Who sent the return?"

It's "What evidence proves who started this return, and why?"

The assumption was:
"The recall was sent, so the case is moving."
Sending a recall proves nothing. Only the answer closes the question.

Why?

A camt.029 answers a camt.056 by stating whether the recall has been accepted or refused. The originator bank cannot close the recall until that response arrives and confirms whether the funds are coming back.

No camt.029 means no closure. Silence is not an answer.

What proves the recall was accepted or refused?

BA Takeaway

Track the recall as open until the camt.029 arrives. Treat an accepted recall as a decision, not as money moved, and wait for the pacs.004 before telling the customer the funds are back.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Recall request sent
→ Response received
→ Funds returned
→ Customer told only on evidence

The real requirement isn't "Has the recall been sent?"

It's "What evidence proves the recall was accepted or refused?"

title: EUR 30,000 returned with a reason code no bank recognised
explain:
EUR 30,000 came back as a pacs.004.
The reason code on it did not exist in the scheme rulebook.
The next bank in the chain rejected the return, and the money sat in limbo.

Here's how that happens:

→ → Payment returned with a pacs.004
→ → Reason code invented by the returning bank
→ → Next bank does not recognise the code
→ → Return rejected, funds stuck

The assumption was:
"Any code that describes the problem will do."
A reason code is a controlled vocabulary, not a free-text field.

Why?

The reason code comes from the bank that refused the payment, and the scheme rulebook lists the codes that bank may use. A bank that invents one risks the return being rejected by the next bank in the chain.

A reason code is a controlled vocabulary, not a free-text field.

What proves this reason code is one the next bank will accept?

BA Takeaway

Use only codes from the scheme rulebook. Check the code against the rulebook before sending, and treat an unrecognised code as a second exception, not a description.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Reason code
→ Rulebook list
→ Next bank acceptance

The real requirement isn't "Does the code describe the problem?"

It's "What evidence proves this reason code is one the next bank will accept?"

Have you ever seen a return rejected because of its reason code?
takeaway: A reason code is a controlled vocabulary, not a free-text field.

title: EUR 95,000 rejected, and the pacs.002 said nothing useful
explain:
A EUR 95,000 pacs.008 was rejected.
The pacs.002 that reported it named the payment and nothing else.
The originator bank spent a day guessing what had gone wrong.

Here's how that happens:

→ → pacs.008 sent for EUR 95,000
→ → Payment rejected
→ → pacs.002 arrives with no status and no reason code
→ → Originator bank guesses at the cause

The assumption was:
"Reporting the rejection is enough."
A report without a reason is a message, not an answer.

Why?

When a pacs.008 is rejected, the pacs.002 must identify the original payment and carry the status and the reason code, so the originator bank knows the payment did not settle and why.

A pacs.002 without status and reason leaves the originator guessing.

What proves why this payment was rejected?

BA Takeaway

Demand the full pacs.002: the original payment identified, the status stated, the reason code carried. Treat a pacs.002 without those fields as incomplete, and chase the missing fields before acting.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Original payment identified
→ Status stated
→ Reason code carried

The real requirement isn't "Was the payment rejected?"

It's "What evidence proves why this payment was rejected?"

Have you ever received a rejection report that explained nothing?
takeaway: A pacs.002 without status and reason leaves the originator guessing.
